item.content:encoded:
Opinion: 341 IS an anomalous object. However, there is nothing that indicates that it should be Securely Contained to Protect anyone. Leaves me a bit torn. Yes, the creator should not have had the knowledge or the technology to create these objects, but similar objects appear IRL from time to time. The Foundation could EASILY dump these in a museum somewhere, and when Science says "But these are impossble!", everyone just throws their hands up and says, "Science also believed in spontaneous generation and the impossibility of bumblebee flight, until we figured out what we got wrong."

However…if the Foundation DID dump these in a museum, and then one or more of them "activated" for reasons unknown…now THAT'D be worth changing my -1 to a +1.

There's a bit of fridge logic to this (if I'm using the term right), just barely enough; how did the person creating these know about how other star systems we never knew about, let alone build them to a scale like this?

That said, it seems innocuous and merely just… here. There's nothing about this, in spirit, that we wouldn't find on the Log of Anomalous Items. This doesn't need some kind of spooky scary story, or something dramatic, but it needs SOMETHING. I like this, I really do. item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
1> What powers them? They RUN by clockwork… but does someone actually wind them up? If APPARENTLY unpowered, that would make them unquestionably an SCP. It would also give further pause to anyone screwing with them.

2> Orbits and relative positions in the system change. Given this, it should be possible to look at the DoomSystem, and project when/if it is representing the state of OUR solar system.
…if the future, it could also be extrapolated back to try and locate the unknown outer planets precisely at THIS time.
…if it's showing NOW… that's a hell of a lot creepier. I'm not quite what that says about things, but it might be worth looking for those outer planets anyway… immediately.

3> The identification of extra-solar systems says the Foundation has a way (sorry, don't know all the SCPs) to see those systems in detail. They could also check the "date" of those systems against their orreries for accuracy/currency.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I like this. It's kind of charming, and the writing really pulled me in. But it just… ends. I got to the end and thought, "That's it?"
As so many have stated before, they don't seem anomalous at all, outside the fact they were created before some of those star systems were discovered by the scientific community at large. But that's pretty easily explained: the maker had a telescope far better than any at the time, no one knew about it, and he made the things. The telescope got destroyed in a fire or whatever, and astronomy was set back a century or two because the blueprints for it were also lost, and discoveries in that vein of technology had to begin anew.

I can't bring myself to downvote because I do just like the entry, but I can't upvote it because it doesn't fit as a scip for me because it's mundane as is. Possibly maybe kinda sorta unusual origin, but in theory can be plausibly explained since nothing else seems weird about them.

As for the "OHHHH! It's just THAT classified!" argument… Things that are so classified absolutely none of the "real" info goes into the article don't really belong on this site, imo. I see the whole point of the SCP Foundation wiki to be seeing "under the hood" of this fictional organization containing crazy stuff. I like some of the articles that are covers for the "real" story, but they also have that story as part of the article, as if the reader has a higher clearance allowing them to see the truth behind the truth of Anomalous Item X. This doesn't have that, so trying to explain it that way just makes it boring to me.

Another way to put it: This is what the Level 1-2 Researchers would see. I feel like the general wiki should read as though Level 3, 4, or possibly even 5, Researchers are looking at the documents after initial redaction (where applicable) has taken place or something, and 341 doesn't treat it that way.

Like I said, no downvote, but it's missing something that would push it to an upvote for me.

item.content:encoded:
Crosslinked and ran across this while researching for my first SCP, and felt obliged to comment after seeing all of the "IT's not a SCP" comments. There has to be a reason why this is classified, but someone is smart enough to see the implications of SCP-341 having anomalous properties, and is reinforced by this phrase:

The exhibition hall of Reliquary Research and Containment Site-76 has SCP-341 on display for all Research and Command personnel to view.

[emphasis added]

It's all implied, but someone competent realized the implications if the other wheels can do something, and doesn't want to risk sparking a SCP-1322 incident. There's no discussion because apparently research staff is smart enough to not touch it, put it on display, and classify it safe before some researcher tries to do something to a neighboring star system.

Could be bit better if someone was studying to see if the wheel of doom is geared, and if so when the population of earth needed to be relocated, but that'd subtract from the mystery and fridge horror.

item.content:encoded:
I agree with Sigma and many others who have commented here. Things like these orreries, things that seem to have been created using knowledge that should not have been available at the time of their creation, actually exist in real life. For example, there's the Antitykthera mechanism, a clockwork device of probable Greek design, built to calculate the positions of stars for navigation at sea, initially believed to have been too complex to have existed at the time. There's also the ruins of Göbekli Tepe, which are dated to around 9000 BC and predate the invention of farming, animal husbandry, the wheel, metallurgy, and writing, yet include massive stone pillars and carvings of animals that would require a staggering amount of labor, especially without the aid of metal tools.

These things aren't anomalous so much as they just redefine our understanding of human history. -1.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
We have some things like that though, and those are SCPs too. The point is, if someone with enough astronomical know-how in the public got ahold of these, they'd eventually realize, "Wait, this thing was made over a hundred years ago, before we had the technology to see [insert star system here], and yet they're perfect in detail. How is that possible?" They fly in the face of physics and/or history as we understand them, and a layperson with these in hand would be able to discover that reality isn't as cut-and-dry as we'd like to believe. To me, that's pretty much the definition of an SCP object.
Also, I love the "ring of doom" bit at the end. Even more reason to keep these away from the public, especially astronomers who would be able to realize -exactly- what these things represent.

I know this is a fairly old and well-liked article, by the way, but I feel this article could do with a bit of a go-over and minor tweaking from a pro astronomer. There are some choices of vocabulary that I feel don't belong at best and are tone-breaking at worst. (Most jarring example: Nobody actually refers to the sun as "Sol" except for science fiction writers.)

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Hrm. -EX is for explained SCPs right?

… Wouldn't that necessitate some explanation of how the creator of these created apparently accurate orreries of far-off star systems that they wouldn't have actually known about or been able to plot?

I'm not saying it's a bad idea at all, just seems like to be an Explained SCP, they'd need an explanation of how they came to exist in the first place, even if it's just that they found out who made them, researched his life, and found out he was amazingly accurate at making various predictions, had an active imagination that happened to match up with reality quite often, or something like that. Maybe he was just a genius at interpreting stellar phenomenon who was just never recognized for his potential and the "ring of doom" was his final creation and an expression of his dissatisfaction at feeling ignored, that would even add an extra bit of melancholy flair to the SCP.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
On the other hand, what resources would they really have to expend on these? A small room with a couple of shelves? Hardly back- or budget-breaking. Arguably the only actual resource they would be consuming would be an SCP number, and there are only self-imposed limits of those, and an unlimited resource can't really be considered to be being consumed in that way.

Agree though that some research logs to give these things some more strange, anachronistic, confounding, or amazing traits would not go unwanted, though. Nothing too big, but something to make them worthy of actual study instead of just sticking them on a shelf.

Either way I think it's fine, but it would be better with giving these some strange properties. It might risk turning them into a copy of the little wind-up stars-and-date box but I think it'd be a worthy risk to take.

Others might remark that the idea that the orreries are very old is enough, but then this could be applied to anything that requires modern technology. Oh look, it's a working cellphone, but it's been found in the sarcophagus of a Pharaoh!…

I'm sorry, but I don't feel this article adds anything to the site. It's well written and the tone is great, but there is absolutely no idea or "catch" to it. Downvote.
